before.title: 12V Auxiliary Battery Premature Failure
before.description: Legacy Model X vehicles use a small 12V lead-acid auxiliary battery (AtlasBX/Hankook 85B24LS, 45Ah) that powers low-voltage systems. It commonly degrades in 2-4 years and can fail with little warning. When it dies, the car may not wake/start, doors may lock out, screens go dead, and charging can be blocked. A 'Replace 12V battery soon' / '12V battery needs service' alert typically precedes total failure by only days.
before.solution: Replace the 12V battery promptly when the warning appears (do not wait weeks). Use the OEM AtlasBX/Hankook 85B24LS or a quality equivalent; many owners upgrade to a lithium replacement (e.g., Ohmmu) for longer life. Keep the car on a low-voltage-friendly maintenance routine. Note BMS DTCs BMS_f151/BMS_w151 or GTW_w017 indicate the 12V system is failing.

before.title: Air Suspension Leak, Sagging Ride Height & Compressor Failure
before.description: The Model X's standard adaptive air suspension develops air leaks at the air struts, fittings, or valve block, plus compressor wear, causing a corner (usually a front) to sag overnight, slow self-leveling, and 'suspension will not raise / needs service' warnings. Height-sensor faults can mimic a leak by commanding bleed-down. Compressor failure is often driven by moisture ingress causing internal rust or winter freezing.
before.solution: Diagnose the pattern first: confirm which corner drops, soap-test struts/lines for leaks, verify compressor build pressure and duty cycle, and check height-sensor plausibility before buying parts. Repairs range from replacing a leaking air strut/spring or valve block to a new air suspension compressor. Replace the compressor's air dryer to prevent repeat moisture failures.
symptoms: 'Suspension will not raise' / needs service alert
Slow leveling or won't reach set height
Compressor runs constantly or is noisy

fixParts.note: Fits front L or R. OEM 1027361-00-G is the common revision for 2016-2020; early-build cars (before ~Oct 2016) used 1027361-00-E. This is the primary part when the leak/sag is at a front corner. 2021-2023 refresh cars use later revisions of the same base 1027361 number.
fixParts.component: Front air strut / air spring assembly (leaking corner sag repair)

fixParts.note: Fits rear L or R (Sep 2015-Feb 2021 coverage on -00-G). Use when a rear corner is the one dropping overnight. 2021-2023 refresh uses a later part (e.g. 1620462-00-A) — do NOT use that number on 2016-2020 cars.
fixParts.component: Rear air spring strut assembly (leaking corner sag repair)

fixParts.note: Compressor for weak build-pressure / high duty-cycle / freeze-failure. The Tesla compressor unit ships with the air dryer integrated and includes a new relay; the relay should be replaced with the compressor. Arnott P-3509 covers 2016-Oct 2019 Model X. Alt OEM 1044911-00-D is a shared Model S/X comp
fixParts.component: Air suspension compressor (with integrated air dryer + relay)

fixParts.note: Distributes air to each corner and holds the pressure sensor; replace when the block leaks/bleeds a corner down or fails to hold pressure. Same 1027919-00-B block is shared across Model S/X of this era.
fixParts.component: Air suspension solenoid valve block / manifold (with pressure sensor)

fixParts.note: Front RH = 1027946-00-A, front LH = 1027941-00-A. A faulty height sensor can mimic a leak by commanding bleed-down, so the FIX calls for a plausibility check before parts. Shared with Model S 2012-2021.
fixParts.component: Front ride-height sensor (rules out sensor-commanded bleed-down)

fixParts.note: Rear RH = 1027976-00-A, rear LH = 1027971-00-A. Diagnose alongside the front sensors when a corner drops but no physical leak is found. Shared Model S/X 2016-2021.
fixParts.component: Rear ride-height sensor (rules out sensor-commanded bleed-down)

before.title: Electronic Power Steering Assist Loss (Recall)
before.description: Tesla recalled 40,000+ Model S and Model X vehicles from 2017-2021 because the electronic power steering assist can suddenly stop working after hitting a pothole or driving on rough roads, causing a sudden increase in steering effort and higher crash risk. A separate earlier recall covered pre-October-2016 cars where power-steering mounting bolts corrode in cold/salt climates.
before.solution: Confirm your VIN against the NHTSA/Tesla recall and get the free remedy (an over-the-air firmware calibration update and/or hardware inspection at a service center). Do not ignore a 'power steering assist reduced' warning; the car remains steerable but requires much greater effort. Repairs under recall are free regardless of age or mileage.
symptoms: Loss of assist after a pothole or bump
Steering effort increases at low speed

before.title: Model X Falcon-Wing Door Faults
before.description: The signature Falcon-Wing rear doors on Model X are notoriously trouble-prone — symptoms include doors refusing to open, opening too slowly, getting stuck mid-cycle, mis-detecting obstacles, hitting low ceilings, and squeaking. Tesla revised door hardware multiple times (Gen 1 → Gen 2 → Gen 3 latch mechanism). Issue persists across years but Gen 3 (post-2019) is noticeably more reliable.
before.solution: Tesla service centers can recalibrate doors free if symptoms present; out-of-warranty hardware replacement can be $1,500-$3,000 per door. Latch assembly $400-$800 part; replacement procedure is involved. Sometimes "manual close" mode is a temporary workaround.

before.title: First-Row Seat Belt Anchor May Detach (Recall)
before.description: Tesla recalled 15,000+ Model S and Model X vehicles (Model X built Sept 8, 2021-June 24, 2023) because front-row seat belts may not be properly connected to their pretensioner anchors. During certain prior repairs the belt was disconnected from the pretensioner and not correctly reattached, so the belt could detach in a crash and fail to restrain the occupant, greatly increasing injury risk.
before.solution: Check your VIN against the recall and schedule the free inspection; Tesla verifies and, if needed, reconnects the first-row seat-belt anchors to the pretensioners. Until inspected, ensure belts click firmly and pull-test them. The remedy is provided at no charge.

before.title: Front Door Auto-Presenting Handle Fails to Present / Retract
before.description: The Model X's motorized front-door handles (which auto-present as you approach and retract when driving) frequently jam, fail to extend, or present but won't unlatch the door. Root causes include worn handle drive gears, debris, a jammed retraction mechanism, or a failed door pop actuator. Owners are locked out or trapped-in until they use the app or interior manual release, and lemon-law complaints span 2019-2023+.
before.solution: Run the door-handle calibration in the touchscreen (requires software 2023.12+) and reboot the computer as a first step. Persistent failures require replacing the handle drive unit/actuator gears or the exterior release module. In the meantime, open with the Tesla app or the interior manual release. Keep firmware current, as several handle bugs were addressed in software.
symptoms: Handle presents but door won't open
Handle stuck extended or won't retract
Must use app or manual release to enter

before.title: Front Upper Control Arm Clunk & Premature Suspension Wear
before.description: Model X front (and to a lesser extent rear) control arm assemblies are widely reported to prematurely wear, loosen, or crack. The most common complaint is a clunking or creaking noise from the front suspension over bumps, traced to water intrusion into the upper control arm ball joint / bushing. Owners and a class-action complaint allege the fore and aft links wear early; in severe cases a failed control arm compromises steering stability. The heavy curb weight of the Model X accelerates ball-joint and bushing wear versus lighter EVs.
before.solution: Have the front upper and lower fore/aft links inspected for play and torn bushings when any clunk or creak develops. before.title: Large Drive Unit Bearing Whine / Motor Failure
before.description: Earlier Model X drive units can develop a progressive hum, whine, or drone that rises with road speed, caused by worn rotor bearings inside the motor (the bearings spin up to ~22,000 RPM). The noise is present regardless of throttle position and independent of road surface, distinguishing it from tire noise. Left unaddressed, bearing wear can escalate to full drive-unit failure. Tesla historically replaces the complete unit rather than the bearing.
before.solution: Have the noise diagnosed early: a specialist can sometimes replace the worn bearings with ceramic units for a fraction of a full swap. If caught late, Tesla replaces the complete Large Drive Unit (roughly $5,000-$9,000 out of warranty). Drive-unit failures within the 8yr/unlimited-mile powertrain warranty are covered. Address any speed-correlated whine before it worsens.

before.title: MCU1 eMMC Flash Memory Failure (Black/Frozen Center Screen)
before.description: Early Model X vehicles (built before March 2018) use a Media Control Unit (MCU1) with an 8GB eMMC flash chip rated for only ~3,000 write cycles. Constant logging wears the chip out, degrading memory segments until the central touchscreen freezes, reboots repeatedly, or goes fully black. A dead MCU takes down climate control, navigation, backup camera, charging control, and phone-key access. NHTSA pressured Tesla into a recall covering this defect.
before.solution: Eligible cars qualify for Tesla's 8GB eMMC recall, which replaces the failing chip with a 64GB eMMC free of charge (approx. 90 minutes for Model X). Out-of-recall or out-of-warranty owners can use third-party eMMC daughterboard replacement/repair services, or upgrade to MCU2. Reducing unnecessary logging and dashcam writes can slow wear.

before.title: Panoramic Windshield Cracking & Delamination
before.description: The Model X's oversized one-piece panoramic windshield (the largest in production) is prone to cracking from minor rock/stone impacts and to delamination (bubbling/cloudy separation between glass layers), sometimes starting at the edges. Because the glass is huge, curved, and integrates the wiper and sensor mounts, replacement is expensive and often has long parts lead times. Some delamination cases have been covered under warranty as a manufacturing defect.
before.solution: Small chips outside the driver's critical vision area can sometimes be resin-repaired if addressed immediately. Cracks and any delamination require full windshield replacement using an OEM panoramic unit and recalibration of the forward camera/ADAS. Document delamination early and pursue warranty/goodwill coverage; a quality PPF or windshield film reduces future chip risk.
symptoms: Crack spreading from a small chip
Bubbling or cloudy patch in glass

before.title: Phantom Braking on Autopilot / Full Self-Driving
before.description: Model X vehicles using Autopilot or FSD have reported 'phantom braking' - sudden, unprompted hard braking or deceleration when no obstacle is present. With radar removed from post-2021 cars (Tesla Vision, camera-only), shadows, glare, overpasses, and oncoming traffic can trigger false automatic emergency braking. It was part of a large software recall and a multi-year NHTSA investigation (since closed as incidents declined with software updates).
before.solution: Keep the car on the latest firmware, which progressively reduced phantom-braking events. Report recurring events to Tesla so they are logged. Drivers should keep hands on the wheel and be ready to override with the accelerator. No hardware repair is required; the remedy is delivered as over-the-air software updates (free).
symptoms: Sudden unexpected braking with no obstacle
Speed drops on Autopilot without input

before.title: Touchscreen Yellow Border / Band Discoloration
before.description: A yellow band or border develops around the perimeter of the center touchscreen. It is not a failed LCD but a breakdown of the adhesive/laminate layer bonding the display, aggravated by heat and UV exposure. It affects both MCU1 and MCU2 units and is largely cosmetic, though widespread and persistent. Some owners report recurrence after repair.
before.solution: Tesla's fix is a UV-light fixture treatment that cures the discolored adhesive in ~2-3 hours; it is free during the warranty period but requires a service center with the UV tool (cannot be done by mobile service). Owners out of warranty can use DIY/third-party UV curing kits. Full display replacement is only needed if UV treatment fails to hold.
symptoms: Yellow band around edge of touchscreen
